chapter: Stagg's own story and the promotional society
title: Stagg's youth and record collecting, 1948-1957
summary: Stagg recalls buying his first Armstrong record, collecting British and American records, his first concerts in Croydon, and specializing in New Orleans music.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: My... I first became interested in traditional style jazz while I was still at school. I was born in 1938. This was in about 1948, 49. The first record I ever bought was Louis Armstrong's Basin Street Blues, which I bought second hand at some ridiculous price of about eight shillings at that time, was a hell of a lot of money. I was doing a paper round and had seen this record in a post office, and had saved for about four weeks to buy this record, and hoping it hadn't gone. I used to go down and look at this record for about four weeks before I could afford to buy it. I bought this record and it was overjoyed. This was the very first record I'd ever heard. This was, as I say, by Louis Armstrong. I went on from there, decided I would buy some of this music on record. And I bought a few Humphrey Littleton 78s, and eventually, I think it was for a birthday or part of a birthday present, I bought one of the first LPs by the Humphrey Littleton band. I can recall it was called Humphrey the Conway, and the Conway Hall was a hall in Red Lion Square, London, where they used to hold early Humphrey Littleton band concerts. At that time, I went further and went on and on and bought every record I could afford to buy by every band imaginable. This was before I decided to specialise in just New Orleans music. There was no New Orleans music as such then. They were all bands such as the Armstrong 78s and the British bands. We'd only heard of George Lewis and Bunk Johnson in those days. There were no records about them, although very, very few and far between. The first jazz concert I went to was at the Civic Hall in Croydon, and I saw the Ian Bell Band and the Red River Band. The Ian Bell Band were an offshoot of the George Webb Dixielanders. I only ever saw George Webb's Dixielanders once in person. It was about the same time, just before they broke up. It must have been about 1950, 51, just before the band finished. Most of the musicians joined either the Ian Bell Band or some other small bands around at that time. These concerts were held once a month in Croydon, and I don't think I missed one between 1950 and about 1954. Still collecting records all the time. About 1955 I had such a tremendous collection of odd records that I decided to specialise in just New Orleans music. Excluding the long-term expatriates like Armstrong and Kid Orry, mainly for the reason at that time, and it still applies today, is that through lack of money there was so much music about of one sort that to specialise you had to cut out the other types of jazz, which I still have to today. Not because of any dislike, but the preference is and always has been. I can remember going down to a local record store in Croydon, England, and taking all these great heap of 78s and a few LPs down there of the British stuff and selling them or part exchanging them for what all the music I could get.
